# Vocabulary-driven generation

The source vocabulary contains alternatives of token sequences. The generic product
chooses one alternative per slot and concatenates tokens; rendering happens last.
An empty alternative is `[]`, not a token containing a space.

```shen
(define v.colors
  {--> (list (list string))}
  -> [["amber"] ["violet"]])

(define v.objects
  {--> (list (list string))}
  -> [["kite"] ["cup"]])

(define v.extended-colors
  {--> (list (list string))}
  -> (append (v.colors) [["teal"]]))

(define v.product
  {(list (list (list string))) --> (list (list string))}
  [] -> [[]]
  [Choices | Slots] ->
    (let Rest (v.product Slots)
      (mapcan (/. Choice (map (/. Words (append Choice Words)) Rest)) Choices)))

(define v.render
  {(list string) --> string}
  [] -> ""
  [Word] -> Word
  [Word | Words] -> (@s Word " " (v.render Words)))

(define v.phrases
  {(list (list string)) --> (list string)}
  Colors -> (map (fn v.render) (v.product [Colors (v.objects)])))

(define v.distinct?
  {(list A) --> boolean}
  [] -> true
  [X | Xs] -> (and (not (element? X Xs)) (v.distinct? Xs)))

(define v.assert
  {boolean --> boolean}
  true -> true
  false -> (error "vocabulary assertion failed"))

(v.assert (= (v.phrases (v.colors))
             ["amber kite" "amber cup" "violet kite" "violet cup"]))
(v.assert (v.distinct? (v.phrases (v.colors))))
(v.assert (= (v.phrases (v.extended-colors))
             ["amber kite" "amber cup" "violet kite" "violet cup" "teal kite" "teal cup"]))
(v.assert (v.distinct? (v.phrases (v.extended-colors))))
(v.assert (= (map (fn v.render) (v.product [[[] ["amber"]] [["kite"]]]))
             ["kite" "amber kite"]))
(v.assert (= (map (fn v.render) (v.product [[["amber"]] [[]]])) ["amber"]))
(v.assert (= (map (fn v.render) (v.product [[[]] [[]]])) [""]))
(v.assert (= (v.product [[]]) []))
```

The extension changes only source vocabulary: it appends the `teal` alternative;
no derived phrase is added to the generator. Expected outputs above are test
oracles, not implementation data. By induction on slots, the base product contains
the one empty choice, and the step enumerates every choice paired with every
suffix. Thus the two finite slots yield 2×2 and 3×2 results. Uniqueness assumes
distinct alternatives and unambiguous rendering (here single, nonempty words with
no embedded spaces). The generic product does not promise deduplication for
arbitrary vocabularies. Empty alternatives skip a slot; empty *strings* inside a
nonempty token list are outside the spacing convention. Shape types do not prove
this completeness or uniqueness argument. No trusted declarations are used.

# Indexed persistent history

Newest items live at the front of a plain immutable list. The index is a
structural term, not an arithmetic claim. These are representation rules and
checked implementation bodies, not axioms asserting operation signatures.

```shen
(datatype h.history
  __________________________
  [] : (h.history hz A);

  X : A; Xs : (h.history N A);
  ========================================
  [X | Xs] : (h.history (hs N) A);)

(define h.empty
  {--> (h.history hz A)}
  -> [])

(define h.append
  {A --> (h.history N A) --> (h.history (hs N) A)}
  X H -> [X | H])

(define h.newest
  {(h.history (hs N) A) --> A}
  [X | _] -> X)

(define h.remove
  {(h.history (hs N) A) --> (h.history N A)}
  [_ | H] -> H)

(define h.double-newest
  {(h.history (hs N) number) --> (h.history (hs N) number)}
  [X | H] -> [(* 2 X) | H])

(define h.assert
  {boolean --> boolean}
  true -> true
  false -> (error "history assertion failed"))

(let Old (h.append 7 (h.empty))
  (let New (h.append 11 Old)
    (let Replaced (h.double-newest New)
      (do (h.assert (= (h.newest Old) 7))
          (h.assert (= (h.newest New) 11))
          (h.assert (= (h.newest Replaced) 22))
          (h.assert (= (h.remove New) Old))
          (h.assert (= (h.remove Replaced) Old))
          (h.assert (= (h.remove (h.remove Replaced)) (h.empty)))
          (h.assert (= (h.newest (h.remove Replaced)) 7))))))
```

Reading empty is rejected:

<!-- reject: h.bad-empty-read -->
```shen
(define h.bad-empty-read
  {--> number}
  -> (h.newest (h.empty)))
```

Removing the only item leaves no newest item:

<!-- reject: h.bad-after-remove -->
```shen
(define h.bad-after-remove
  {--> number}
  -> (h.newest (h.remove (h.append 7 (h.empty)))))
```

A dishonest implementation cannot claim growth:

<!-- reject: h.bad-growth -->
```shen
(define h.bad-growth
  {A --> (h.history N A) --> (h.history (hs N) A)}
  X H -> H)
```

The replacement signature fixes the length index; its checked body reconstructs
one cell with the original predecessor. The index alone does not establish that
it doubles the value or preserves the *same* predecessor: the body and assertions
supply that evidence. Persistence follows from immutable list construction and
is exercised by retaining the old values. No mutation, operation declarations,
or untyped boundary is used. These are open datatype rules: the claims assume no
later hostile extensions or redefinitions. Indices alone do not prove ordering,
purity, or termination of arbitrary future operations.

# Cyclic prerequisites

Use Prolog facts and simple-path search, not unrestricted transitive recursion.
`Seen` initially contains the queried job. Each edge extends it, so neither the
input itself nor any already visited vertex can be returned on that path.

`defprolog` is an explicitly untyped boundary in Shen. The single exported
`q.raw` declaration below is trusted; its symbol/list contract is not inferred
from the Prolog body. Call it only with a ground symbol. The finite static facts
and the groundness discipline are part of the termination argument.

<!-- untyped -->
```shen
(defprolog q.edge
  compile seed <--;
  package compile <--;
  publish package <--;
  seed package <--;)

(defprolog q.path
  X Y Seen <-- (q.edge X Y)
               (when (not (element? Y Seen)));
  X Y Seen <-- (q.edge X Z)
               (when (not (element? Z Seen)))
               (q.path Z Y [Z | Seen]);)

(define q.raw
  Job -> (prolog? (findall R (q.path (receive Job) R [(receive Job)]) Rs)
                 (return Rs)))

(declare q.raw [symbol --> [list symbol]])
```

```shen
(define q.nub
  {(list A) --> (list A)}
  [] -> []
  [X | Xs] -> (q.nub Xs) where (element? X Xs)
  [X | Xs] -> [X | (q.nub Xs)])

(define q.requirements
  {symbol --> (list symbol)}
  Job -> (q.nub (q.raw Job)))

(define q.subset?
  {(list A) --> (list A) --> boolean}
  [] _ -> true
  [X | Xs] Ys -> (and (element? X Ys) (q.subset? Xs Ys)))

(define q.assert
  {boolean --> boolean}
  true -> true
  false -> (error "prerequisite assertion failed"))

(define q.expect
  {symbol --> (list symbol) --> boolean}
  Job Expected ->
    (let Got (q.requirements Job)
      (do (q.assert (q.subset? Got Expected))
          (q.assert (q.subset? Expected Got))
          (q.assert (= (length Got) (length Expected)))
          (q.assert (not (element? Job Got))))))

(q.expect publish [package compile seed])
(q.expect seed [package compile])
(q.expect docs [])
```

`docs` is an isolated job: it needs no edge fact and has no reachable vertex.
Output order is intentionally unspecified. `nub` removes duplicates across
paths, while `Seen` prevents repeats within a path. A finite graph has only
finitely many simple paths; every reachable distinct vertex has a simple path,
so restricting traversal this way remains complete, including in this cycle.
The tests compare sets and cardinalities, not engine enumeration order.

The only negation is the Shen Boolean `not` on `element?`, after the edge has
bound its endpoint and with a ground `Seen` list. It is a decidable ground
membership test, not a claim about unbound Prolog variables or an open-world
absence of edges. Unground/reverse queries are not supported by this interface.
Types do not prove graph reachability, finiteness, or declaration soundness.

# Typed expression grammar

Two grammar levels give multiplication precedence. Each level parses a head
and a list of following operands, then folds left with checked semantic actions.
The token union admits heterogeneous number/operator lists without pretending
they are homogeneous symbol lists. No parse-result declaration is trusted.

```shen
(datatype p.token
  N : number;
  ______________
  N : p.token;

  if (element? S [plus times])
  __________________________
  S : p.token;)

(datatype p.expr
  N : number;
  ______________
  N : p.expr;

  L : p.expr; R : p.expr;
  ===============================
  [p-add L R] : p.expr;

  L : p.expr; R : p.expr;
  ===============================
  [p-mul L R] : p.expr;)

(datatype p.number-refinement
  ______________________________________
  (number? X) : verified >> X : number;)

(datatype p.refine-if
  Test : boolean; Test : verified >> X : A; (not Test) : verified >> Y : A;
  ______________________________________________________________________
  (if Test X Y) : A;)

(define p.adds
  {p.expr --> (list p.expr) --> p.expr}
  Acc [] -> Acc
  Acc [X | Xs] -> (p.adds [p-add Acc X] Xs))

(define p.muls
  {p.expr --> (list p.expr) --> p.expr}
  Acc [] -> Acc
  Acc [X | Xs] -> (p.muls [p-mul Acc X] Xs))

(defcc <p-expr>
  {(list p.token) ==> p.expr}
  <p-term> <p-plus-tail> := (p.adds <p-term> <p-plus-tail>);)

(defcc <p-plus-tail>
  {(list p.token) ==> (list p.expr)}
  plus <p-term> <p-plus-tail> := [<p-term> | <p-plus-tail>];
  <e> := [];)

(defcc <p-term>
  {(list p.token) ==> p.expr}
  <p-factor> <p-times-tail> := (p.muls <p-factor> <p-times-tail>);)

(defcc <p-times-tail>
  {(list p.token) ==> (list p.expr)}
  times <p-factor> <p-times-tail> := [<p-factor> | <p-times-tail>];
  <e> := [];)

(defcc <p-factor>
  {(list p.token) ==> p.expr}
  N := N where (number? N);)

(define p.parse
  {(list p.token) --> p.expr}
  Tokens -> (compile (fn <p-expr>) Tokens))

(define p.eval
  {p.expr --> number}
  [p-add L R] -> (+ (p.eval L) (p.eval R))
  [p-mul L R] -> (* (p.eval L) (p.eval R))
  N -> N where (number? N)
  _ -> (error "invalid expression"))

(define p.rejects?
  {(list p.token) --> boolean}
  Tokens -> (trap-error (do (p.parse Tokens) false) (/. E true)))

(define p.assert
  {boolean --> boolean}
  true -> true
  false -> (error "parser assertion failed"))

(p.assert (= (p.parse [2 plus 3 times 4]) [p-add 2 [p-mul 3 4]]))
(p.assert (= (p.eval (p.parse [2 plus 3 times 4])) 14))
(p.assert (= (p.parse [1 plus 2 plus 3]) [p-add [p-add 1 2] 3]))
(p.assert (= (p.parse [2 times 3 times 4]) [p-mul [p-mul 2 3] 4]))
(p.assert (= (p.eval (p.parse [1 plus 2 plus 3 times 4 times 5])) 63))
(p.assert (p.rejects? []))
(p.assert (p.rejects? [plus 2]))
(p.assert (p.rejects? [2 plus]))
(p.assert (p.rejects? [2 times plus 3]))
(p.assert (p.rejects? [2 3]))
(p.assert (p.rejects? [2 plus 3 4]))
```

`compile` is used at the public boundary, rather than invoking a nonterminal
and ignoring its remainder: it requires complete consumption. Trailing valid
tokens are tested explicitly. Failure raises an error, which `p.rejects?` catches
only in the negative tests. Input is already tokenized; unknown token symbols
are outside the typed input domain. There are no parentheses or unary operators.

The checked grammar actions and folds establish AST shape; the `number?`
verified rule is the standard guard refinement and depends on that predicate's
meaning. The general `if` rule propagates verified guards from generated grammar
code. These are explicit type-system extensions, not untyped parse-result axioms.
Types alone do not prove precedence, associativity, complete consumption,
unambiguity, parser termination, or arithmetic correctness. AST-shape tests matter
because evaluation of associative operators alone cannot detect grouping errors.

# Configured transition and a separate private counter

An account configuration captures only a fee value. Balance is an explicit input;
there is no account cell. Credit has no fee; debit charges amount plus fee only
on success. Negative fees, balances, and action amounts raise domain errors.
Numbers use the runtime's arithmetic; this is not a decimal-money implementation.

```shen
(datatype t.action
  Amount : number;
  ==========================
  [credit Amount] : t.action;

  Amount : number;
  =========================
  [debit Amount] : t.action;)

(datatype t.result
  Balance : number;
  =========================
  [t-ok Balance] : t.result;

  ______________________________
  insufficient-funds : t.result;)

(define t.apply
  {number --> number --> t.action --> t.result}
  Fee Balance [credit Amount] -> [t-ok (+ Balance Amount)]
    where (and (>= Fee 0) (>= Balance 0) (>= Amount 0))
  Fee Balance [debit Amount] ->
    (let Cost (+ Amount Fee)
      (if (>= Balance Cost) [t-ok (- Balance Cost)] insufficient-funds))
    where (and (>= Fee 0) (>= Balance 0) (>= Amount 0))
  _ _ _ -> (error "negative fee, balance, or amount"))

(define t.configure
  {number --> (number --> t.action --> t.result)}
  Fee -> (/. Balance (/. Action (t.apply Fee Balance Action))) where (>= Fee 0)
  _ -> (error "negative fee"))

(define t.assert
  {boolean --> boolean}
  true -> true
  false -> (error "transition assertion failed"))

(let LowFee (t.configure 2)
  (let HighFee (t.configure 5)
    (let Before 100
      (do (t.assert (= (LowFee Before [debit 10]) [t-ok 88]))
          (t.assert (= (HighFee Before [debit 10]) [t-ok 85]))
          (t.assert (= (LowFee Before [credit 10]) [t-ok 110]))
          (t.assert (= (HighFee Before [credit 10]) [t-ok 110]))
          (t.assert (= (LowFee Before [debit 10]) (LowFee Before [debit 10])))
          (t.assert (= Before 100))
          (t.assert (= (LowFee 11 [debit 10]) insufficient-funds))
          (t.assert (= (HighFee 14 [debit 10]) insufficient-funds))
          (t.assert (= (LowFee 12 [debit 10]) [t-ok 0]))
          (t.assert (= (LowFee Before [debit 10]) [t-ok 88]))))))
```

Here is a deliberately different abstraction: a factory allocates a private
one-cell vector, returning only a function that increments it. Calls take a dummy
symbol, so creation and invocation are distinct. This block is typed too; vector
mutation is not hidden behind an asserted pure operation type.

```shen
(define t.counter
  {--> (symbol --> number)}
  -> (let Cell (vector 1)
       (do (vector-> Cell 1 0)
           (/. Tick
             (let Next (+ (<-vector Cell 1) 1)
               (do (vector-> Cell 1 Next) Next))))))

(let First (t.counter)
  (let Alias First
    (let Second (t.counter)
      (do (t.assert (= (First tick) 1))
          (t.assert (= (Alias tick) 2))
          (t.assert (= (Second tick) 1))
          (t.assert (= (First tick) 3))
          (t.assert (= (Second tick) 2))))))
```

Aliases of a single returned function share its cell; a new factory invocation
allocates another cell. Privacy is lexical encapsulation (no vector is returned),
not a capability theorem against runtime introspection. Tests assume sequential
execution; no concurrency or atomicity guarantee is made.

Both account transition and counter have arrow types. Such types say nothing
about mutation, replay, aliasing, fee immutability, arithmetic laws, or allocation
freshness. Those properties come from the respective bodies, closure/vector
semantics, and behavioral assertions. In particular the transition never updates
the predecessor balance, and no call can replace the captured fee. No trusted
declarations or untyped fences are needed; primitives and runtime semantics
remain trusted. Types do not prove overdraft policy or nonnegative results.

# Review of the stack claim

The conclusion does not follow. Datatype axioms over untyped operation names
are a trusted interface, not a check of their implementation bodies. Clients can
prove consequences of a false axiom. A `declare` would have the same limitation.

## Smallest counterexample

Start with `S = empty`, push one value `7`, then ask for the top of the result.
The asserted interface gives `push 7 S : stack number [succ 0]`, so the client
call to `top` typechecks. But the given push body returns `S`, which is still
empty. There is no legitimate newest `7` to return. Depending on the unprovided
empty/top implementation it might fail, loop, or return some bogus default. No
specific execution result is claimed here. A minimal specification test requires
`top (push 7 empty) = 7` and must raise an error on mismatch; an exception is
also a failure, not a pass. This single push suffices to refute the growth claim.

## Repair and evidence

* Fix push to construct a new cell or closure containing the item and the old
  stack. Do not mutate the old stack if persistence is required.
* Prefer a structural representation with an empty base rule and a double-line
  cons rule indexed by successor. Give **implementation bodies** signatures for
  empty, push, top, and pop. Then `push X S -> S` must be rejected as claiming a
  successor index while returning the old index. Check this deliberately wrong
  implementation, not merely a wrong client.
* Add negative clients for top-of-empty and top-after-popping-a-singleton. Add
  positive assertions for top-after-push, LIFO order with two distinct values,
  pop restoring the predecessor, and retained old versions staying unchanged.
  These are finite tests, not universal proofs.
* If opaque untyped closures must remain, minimize and explicitly document the
  trusted boundary. Validate it with model-based tests against immutable lists,
  implementation review, or a separate simulation proof. Publishing operation
  axioms alone cannot discharge those obligations.

## What the indices actually establish

With sound representation rules and checked bodies, these signatures can track
structural length and make top require a nonempty stack. They do not specify
which element top returns, that push stores its argument, or which predecessor
pop restores. An implementation could keep the length while reordering or
replacing elements. Ordering needs a content/sequence model or separate laws;
persistence needs old-version preservation; purity needs effect reasoning or
inspection of the operations and their reachable state; termination needs a
well-founded argument or other termination evidence. Shen arrow types and
length indices do not provide these automatically.

Any proof still assumes sound inference rules, correct primitive/runtime
behavior, no hostile datatype extension or redefinition, and sound declarations.
A checked structural repair reduces the trusted surface; it does not turn tests
or those assumptions into theorems. This review is prose only and reports no
invented run of the unprovided closure library.

# Trial report

## Results

All six requested files are in `answers/<task>/SKILL.md`. The final checker run
reported **10 blocks, 0 failed (shen-jit)**: six accepted typed fences, three
expected type rejections, and one explicitly untyped Prolog fence. Review is
prose only. No failed checker attempts or incomplete implementations occurred.

| Task | Mechanism and evidence | Result / remaining obligations |
|---|---|---|
| vocabulary | Typed Cartesian product over source alternatives, token concatenation, edge rendering. Exact original four and extended six strings; explicit distinctness; empty alternatives on either side, both empty, and no choices. | Passed. Completeness follows by induction on finite slots, not from the shape types. Uniqueness assumes the supplied distinct words and unambiguous rendering. Arbitrary vocabularies may duplicate outputs. |
| history | Structural successor-indexed immutable lists; all five operation bodies checked. Persistence, old/new tops, doubled top, predecessor equality and removal to empty asserted. | Passed, including expected rejection of empty read, read after removing singleton, and dishonest growth implementation. Length types alone do not prove content laws, ordering, purity, or termination. |
| prerequisites | Prolog edge facts plus visited simple-path relation; typed deduplication and set/cardinality assertions for publish, seed, docs. | Passed. Finite facts and ground queries justify termination; simple paths preserve reachability. Output order and unknown-job validation are not promised. |
| parser | Typed `defcc`, token union, AST datatype, checked left-fold actions, typed evaluator. Precedence, left-associated ASTs for both operators, repeated mixed operators, empty/malformed inputs, and trailing tokens asserted. | Passed. No trusted parse-result declaration. Typechecking establishes AST shape, not general language correctness, completeness, ambiguity, termination, or arithmetic laws. |
| transition | Typed immutable-fee closure with explicit balance; separate typed vector-backed counter factory. Two fees, replay/interleaving, credit, unchanged predecessor, insufficient funds, exact exhaustion, shared aliases and fresh factory state asserted. | Both fences passed. Purity/replay, lexical privacy and allocation independence are behavioral/body/runtime properties, not arrow-type theorems. Sequential use only; not decimal finance or concurrent counter semantics. |
| review | Prose identifies the unchecked operation axioms, singleton counterexample, structural repair, negative implementation test and content/model obligations. | Completed review. No execution of the unprovided library or invented outcome. |

Every executable assertion raises an error on mismatch. Parser negative tests
catch parse errors; an assertion failure itself is outside that catch. History
negative fences are expected checker rejections and do not accumulate.

## Trusted surfaces

* Only prerequisites uses an untyped fence: Shen's `defprolog` and its query
  wrapper. `(declare q.raw [symbol --> [list symbol]])` is an explicit trusted
  contract, not a checked implementation theorem. Its callers, deduplication and
  tests are checked. Negation is only ground Boolean membership negation after
  edge binding.
* Parser introduces the `number?` verified refinement and a general verified
  `if` rule for grammar guards. Their logical soundness and the stable meaning
  of `number?` are assumptions; no operation signature is asserted over an
  untyped parser.
* All other operation bodies are typed. Structural datatype rules remain part
  of the specification/trusted logic. No hostile extensions or redefinitions are
  assumed. Primitive arithmetic, closure/list/vector behavior, `compile`, and
  the runtime/checker itself remain trusted.
* Finite examples are behavioral evidence, not universal proofs. No formal
  effect, termination, encapsulation, arithmetic or full parser-correctness
  proof is claimed. No performance comparison was made.

## Commands actually run

All commands ran in
`/private/tmp/bifrost-skills-drive/trials/gpt-6.1-sol-original`.
Environment variables selected the supplied runtime and adapters; none were
changed. The following are the exact shell commands, in chronological order.

```bash
pwd; ls -la; find input-skills -type f; env | grep '^BIFROST_'
```

```bash
"$BIFROST_TRIAL_BIN" skills check --help; "$BIFROST_TRIAL_BIN" eval --help; ls -la "$BIFROST_SHEN_JIT"
```

First check, after writing vocabulary, history, prerequisites and parser:

```bash
"$BIFROST_TRIAL_BIN" skills check --impl shen-jit --dir answers
```

Result: 8 blocks, 0 failed.

Second check, after adding transition and review:

```bash
"$BIFROST_TRIAL_BIN" skills check --impl shen-jit --dir answers
```

Result: 10 blocks, 0 failed. A subsequent prose-only clarification in prerequisites
states that unknown ground symbols also return no requirements.

The four supplied `input-skills/*/SKILL.md` files were read with the file-reading
tool, not shell commands. No linked references were needed. File-writing/editing
tools created the six solutions and this report. No other condition, checkout,
prior session, or answer key was read; no delegation, dependency installation,
or runtime/checker modification was performed.
